    AI Overview
    The Strait of Hormuz is a vital, narrow maritime chokepoint (approx. 21–30 miles wide) connecting the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman, located between Iran and Oman. It acts as the world's most significant energy shipping route, with roughly 20% of global oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) passing through it daily. 
    Key Usage Examples and Significance: 
    • Energy Transport: It is the primary route for oil exports from Saudi Arabia, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar, and the UAE, largely bound for Asian markets.
    • Geopolitical Chokepoint: It is frequently used by Iran as a strategic lever to pressure Western powers, often threatening or conducting partial closures/attacks on shipping, as noted in the
      Al Jazeera and The Conversation reports.
    • Military Patrols: As discussed on Wikipedia, U.S. and regional naval forces maintain a constant presence, managing a traffic separation scheme (TSS) for safe passage. 
    Synonyms/Related Terms: 
    • The Hormuz Gateway: Used frequently in historical contexts, such as in this YouTube video.
    • Global Oil Chokepoint: Common description of the area's economic function.
    • The Straits: Often referred to implicitly, as discussed on BBC News and Britannica. 
    It serves as the only sea passage from the Persian Gulf to the open ocean, making it crucial for global economic stability.

    Which country owns the Strait of Hormuz?
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    As of April 2026,
    Iran exerts de facto operational control over the Strait of Hormuz, using its navy and Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) to monitor and restrict traffic, particularly during the 2026 war. Iran's control is bolstered by its control of several islands, including Larak, and its strategic position along the northern coast. 
    Key Details on Control and Authority: 
    • Geographical Control: The Strait is located between Iran and Oman, with both countries maintaining territorial waters. However, Iran dominates the coastline and has built extensive military infrastructure in the region, including on the contested islands of Abu Musa, Greater Tunb, and Lesser Tunb.
    • Operational Control:
      Iran’s IRGC has stated it is in "complete control" of the strait, and began imposing tolls of up to
      million on select vessels to pass during the 2026 war,.
    • Significance: The Strait of Hormuz is a vital maritime choke point, handling roughly 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports.
    • International Stance: While UNCLOS and international law recognize freedom of navigation, Iran has utilized its military presence on nearby islands (e.g., Larak and Qeshm) and naval facilities, like Bandar Abbas, to disrupt shipping. 
    Iran’s control is highly contentious, particularly as it has restricted access for several nations during the recent conflict.

      The Strait of Hormuz is a waterway between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman. On the north coast lies Iran, and on the south coast lies the Musandam Peninsula, shared by the United Arab Emirates and the Musandam Governorate, an exclave of Oman.
